archetype.name: Cup Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose elite forward group and Makar-Toews pairing already outscore nearly everyone, but which is winning this year with finishing and firepower rather than the suffocating defense and goaltending of last season.

report.headline: Still a top-four team by margin, but last year's defensive wall is gone
report.take:
Colorado is 12-6-3 with a +21 goal differential, fourth in the league at a goal a game. That is a contender's margin, and the site's ninth-place rank undersells it slightly. The Avalanche are scoring 4.05 goals a game, second in the league, behind an A+ forward group. Nathan MacKinnon has 30 points and 71 shots in 20 games, and Cale Makar and Devon Toews (+16, 58.8% xGF) make up a top pair ranked sixth and third at their position. The 5-on-5 process is good too: 52.9% xGF (8th) and 53% CF (6th).

The offense, though, is running on more than process. Colorado's skaters are shooting 13.4% in all situations, third in the league and two points above the league's 11.4%, and the 5-on-5 PDO sits at 102.9. Artturi Lehkonen has 15 goals on 46 shots and Martin Necas has 10 on 44. Those are hot-hand numbers, not rates to bank on. Some of the 4.05 goals a game will come back to earth even if the shot volume (30.2 a game, 3rd) holds.

The real change from last year is at the other end. In 2025-26 this team had the league's best defense, a 56.9% xGF and +34.3 goalies GSAx on the way to 121 points. Now it ranks 16th in goals against, allows a league-average 27.2 shots a game and sits at -5.8 GSAx, 28th. The goaltending split explains most of it. Mackenzie Blackwood has been fine (.905, +2.0 GSAx in 15 starts). Scott Wedgewood's six starts have been a disaster (.863, -7.3). Opposing centers are also getting loose, with Colorado 26th at holding them to their usual production.

The pieces roughly cancel. The hot shooting should fade, but so should the bad luck: Colorado's -2.2 Pts vs Goal Diff ranks 28th, a sign the record trails the margin after two overtime losses in the last five games. Expect a team that keeps out-shooting and out-chancing people, scores a bit less, and lands around last year's 100-plus points rather than its 121.

strengths.title: Elite, deep forward group
strengths.body: The forwards grade A+. MacKinnon drives play with 30 points and 71 shots, and Necas, Lehkonen and Kadri all carry real ice time. The production comes from a team that generates the third-most shots in the league, so the volume is sustainable even if the conversion rate isn't.

strengths.title: Makar-Toews top pair controls play
strengths.body: Toews (+16, 58.8% xGF) and Makar (23 points in 19 games, 58.2% xGF) are both top-six at their position and soak up more than 21 minutes a night. They are the main reason Colorado still wins the 5-on-5 chance battle despite a weaker bottom four. Two players of this caliber don't fade on a sample this size.

strengths.title: Record trails the margin
strengths.body: A +21 differential ranks fourth, yet the team sits third in its own division. Pts vs Goal Diff at -2.2 (28th) says close games and overtime have gone against it, including two OT losses in the last five. That kind of misfortune usually evens out.

concerns.title: Backup goaltending is sinking games
concerns.body: Team GSAx is -5.8, 28th, a collapse from +34.3 last season. The damage is concentrated in Wedgewood's six starts at .863 and -7.3 GSAx, while Blackwood is above average. If the backup keeps getting a third of the starts at this level, Colorado can't be the top-tier defense it was.

concerns.title: Shooting luck inflating the offense
concerns.body: Skaters are converting 13.4% of their shots, two points above the league, and the 5-on-5 PDO is 102.9. Lehkonen's 15 goals on 46 shots is the clearest outlier. Expect the scoring rate to drift down even with the shot volume intact.

concerns.title: Centers are getting through
concerns.body: Opposing centers produce 3.24 points a game against Colorado, above their expected 2.83, and the defense ranks 26th at containing them. Centers also take a larger share of the points against than they do league-wide. With a 16th-ranked defense overall, this is a real slippage from last year's league-best unit, not just noise.

trend.note: After a 7-6 October, Colorado has gone 3-0-2 over the last five while allowing just 2.2 goals a game, the tightest defensive stretch of the year. The scoring has eased a little lately while the defense has improved, which is the healthier mix.

weekAhead.headline: Back-to-back against two leaky goaltending teams with dangerous power plays
weekAhead.body:
Colorado plays at Utah on Nov 18 and hosts Anaheim on Nov 19. Both opponents are middling teams with bad goaltending: Utah's .869 save percentage ranks 30th, and Anaheim's .865 ranks 31st with an F grade in net. For a team putting 30.2 shots a game on goal, that is a good setup to keep scoring even as its own shooting cools.

The threat in both games is the power play. Anaheim's 35.2% ranks first and Utah's 34.7% second, against a Colorado kill that is solid at 81% but not elite. Utah is also a real 5-on-5 team (56.8% xGF, 2nd), so the first game is closer than the records suggest. Anaheim, at 46.3% xGF and 29th in goals against, is the softer half. The back-to-back raises the question of who starts in net, and that question has mattered all season.

keyMatchups.title: Colorado shooters vs. bottom-tier goalies
keyMatchups.body: Utah and Anaheim rank 30th and 31st in save percentage. Colorado's volume plus that goaltending should mean another multi-goal night or two. Anaheim gives up the league's 30th-worst production to forwards, a direct opening for MacKinnon and company.

keyMatchups.title: Penalty kill vs. the top power plays
keyMatchups.body: The league's two best power plays come in back-to-back nights. Colorado's 81% kill ranks 10th, good enough to hold if it stays out of the box. Discipline decides whether these games stay comfortable.

keyMatchups.title: Makar-Toews against Utah's defense
keyMatchups.body: Utah's defense ranks 28th at limiting defensemen's points, and its kill is 27th. Colorado's top pair should have room to create, especially on the power play.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts the second half of the back-to-back: a Wedgewood start against Anaheim's 14.7% shooters is the week's biggest risk.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is very good but not last year's juggernaut. The 5-on-5 shares are top-eight rather than league-best, and the defense and goaltending have fallen from first to the middle of the pack. Expect the scoring to cool from 4.05 a game as the 13.4% shooting regresses. That should be partly offset by the close-game luck turning around and by Blackwood carrying most of the starts at an above-average level. The 105-point pace is a fair central estimate.

The ceiling depends on the crease. If the backup's numbers recover even to ordinary, the goals-against rate falls and this becomes a top-five team again. If not, Colorado is a high-scoring playoff team that is vulnerable in tight games. The Central is crowded: Minnesota is already well ahead and Dallas sits level, so home ice is not a given.
swingFactors: Backup goaltending: how many starts Wedgewood gets and whether his save % recovers
Whether the defense tightens back toward last year's level against centers

confidence.note: 21 games: the shot and chance shares are fairly reliable, but the shooting and goaltending splits are small samples, especially Wedgewood's six starts.
